results.title: Cytokine context shapes antigen-presenting and matrix-producing states of cancer-associated fibroblasts.
results.authorString: Song F, Chen Q, Huang D, Zhang Y, Han D, Rao W, Li M, Gao Y, Zhang R, Zhu H, Wang S, Jiang X, Lin S, Bi D, Zhang H, Wei Q, Qin H.
results.abstractText: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) exhibit remarkable functional heterogeneity, with conserved subtypes observed across diverse malignancies. However, their shared roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment (TME) and their dynamic plasticity remain incompletely understood. In this study, through integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiling across four cancer types, we identified two distinct immunomodulatory CAF states, termed antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) and matrix-producing CAFs (mCAFs). Across multiple solid tumors, apCAFs were associated with enhanced anti-tumor immune features and favorable prognosis, whereas mCAFs were associated with immunosuppressive characteristics and poorer clinical outcomes. Spatial analyses revealed distinct localization patterns of apCAFs and mCAFs within the TME. Functionally, patient-derived apCAFs promoted T-cell migration, proliferation, and activation, whereas mCAFs suppressed these responses in vitro. Pan-cancer analyses further revealed a strong inverse correlation between apCAF and mCAF abundance across tumor tissues. Mechanistically, IFN-γ and TGF-β-associated signaling contexts were linked to distinct CAF transcriptional programs, with IFN-γ promoting apCAF-associated features and TGF-β favoring mCAF-associated features, suggesting a potential role of cytokine context in shaping CAF state heterogeneity. Clinically, apCAFs correlated with favorable immunotherapy response, whereas mCAFs predicted poor therapeutic outcomes. Collectively, these findings identify conserved immunomodulatory CAF subtypes across cancers, reveal distinct cytokine-associated CAF programs, and support stromal reprogramming as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

results.title: HECTD1 Directs HIF-1α to Facilitate Intestinal Inflammation and Carcinogenesis via Promoting Th17 Differentiation and Glycolysis.
results.authorString: Xu S, Han Q, Wang F, Zhang Y, Feng H, Liu K, Luo FX, Yuan F, Zhao X, Yu X, Huang H, Zou Q, Zhao R.
results.abstractText: Targeting glucose metabolism in Th17 cells may be beneficial for treating inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and colitis-associated cancer (CAC), however, the molecular mechanisms orchestrating Th17 cell metabolism remain unclear. Here, we revealed that HECTD1 regulates IGF2BP3-dependent HIF-1α translation to promote Th17 cell glycolysis and differentiation and that HECTD1 expression correlates with IBD and CAC pathogenesis. T-cell-specific deletion of HECTD1 mitigated the severity of colitis and CAC in murine models. RNA-seq revealed enrichment of Th17 differentiation, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and HIF-1 signaling pathways among differentially expressed genes between HECTD1-sufficient and HECTD1-deficient CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells. Consistently, loss of HECTD1 suppressed Th17 cell differentiation both in vitro and in vivo, and suppressed glycolytic metabolism and HIF-1α activity, revealing the mechanism underlying its protective effects against IBD and CAC. Mechanistically, HECTD1 potentiates m<sup>6</sup>A-based HIF-1α translation by mediating IGF2BP3 K63-linked ubiquitination to promote the binding of IGF2BP3 with the translation initiation machinery of Hif1a mRNA. Reciprocally, HIF-1α acts as a key transcription factor that promotes Hectd1 gene expression, establishing a distinct positive feedback loop. Our findings highlight a self-reinforcing feedback mechanism in which HECTD1 and HIF-1α engage in mutual regulation to dictate Th17 cell fate and metabolic reprogramming, providing novel potential IBD and CAC treatments targeting HECTD1.

results.title: Ferroptosis in cancer: molecular mechanisms, tumour microenvironment, therapeutic resistance, and clinical translation.
results.authorString: Dewasi G, Jain S.
results.abstractText: Ferroptosis is a distinct form of regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and oxidative membrane damage, and it differs fundamentally from apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis in its molecular mechanisms and execution pathways. Increasing evidence indicates that ferroptosis plays a pivotal role in cancer biology by regulating tumour initiation, progression, metastasis, therapeutic resistance, and interactions within the tumour microenvironment (TME). Dysregulation of iron metabolism, lipid peroxidation, amino acid metabolism, and antioxidant defence systems, including the System Xc⁻-GSH-GPX4, FSP1-CoQ₁₀, GCH1-BH4, and DHODH pathways, collectively determines cellular susceptibility to ferroptosis. Recent studies have further highlighted the contribution of organelle crosstalk, immune cell regulation, and stromal interactions in shaping ferroptotic responses and tumour evolution. In this review, we comprehensively summarise the molecular mechanisms underlying ferroptosis, its regulatory signalling networks, and the major milestones that have advanced the field. We further discuss the multifaceted role of ferroptosis across diverse malignancies, its influence on epithelial-mesenchymal transition, tumour invasion, metastasis, and immune modulation, and its emerging significance in overcoming resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. In addition, we critically evaluate recent progress in ferroptosis-based therapeutic strategies, including nanomedicine, combination therapies, and translational advances, while highlighting current clinical challenges such as tumour heterogeneity, limited pharmacodynamic biomarkers, and safety concerns. Collectively, ferroptosis represents a promising therapeutic vulnerability that bridges fundamental cancer biology with precision oncology. Continued development of biomarker-guided patient stratification, targeted drug delivery systems, and rational combination strategies is expected to accelerate the clinical translation of ferroptosis-based therapies and improve outcomes for patients with refractory and treatment-resistant cancers.

results.title: Diverse patterns of transcriptional regulation and epigenetic reprogramming within PMDs contribute to ESCC progression by regulating EMT and immunosuppression.
results.authorString: Huang Y, Xue J, Luan X, Zhang H, Ding J, Xu J, Zhao Z, Li Q, Tu K, Wang X, Ge W.
results.abstractText: Partially methylated domains (PMDs) represent extensive genome-wide hypomethylated regions that drive genomic instability and proto-oncogene activation. However, their complex regulatory influence on tumor-specific transcriptional networks remains largely elusive. In this study, we developed a robust computational pipeline to characterize aberrant PMD landscapes across pan-cancer. We specifically focused on the epigenetic features associated with transcriptional dysregulation in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). By analyzing gene expression patterns, we classified PMDs into four distinct classes and revealed that several immunosuppressive genes were recurrently activated within Tumor-PMDs across various cancers. While these PMDs were generally marked by elevated repressive H3K27me3 and diminished active histone modifications, the activated genes within them paradoxically exhibited a precise, localized enrichment of H3K9ac and H3K27ac near their transcription start sites (TSSs). This localized epigenetic rewiring suggests a potential correlation where collaborative histone modification landscapes may shape oncogenic chromatin remodeling to license transcriptional dysregulation. Furthermore, we identified a robust co-expression axis between the prognostic gene ATP6V0D2 and established immune checkpoints (HAVCR2, TDO2). Elevated ATP6V0D2 expression was found to potentially contribute to ESCC progression and poor prognosis by activating the complement system and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathways. Capitalizing on these findings, virtual screening and in vitro validation suggested that caffeic acid could act as a potential ATP6V0D2-binding compound, effectively suppressing the migration and viability of ESCC cells. This study further nominates caffeic acid as a candidate compound for further mechanistic and therapeutic investigation in ESCC.
